warmup.q: The transfer API gets 2,000 requests a second. Each spends about 150 ms waiting on the fraud service and almost nothing anywhere else. With one thread per request, about how many threads are busy at once?
warmup.why: Little's law from The thread-per-request wall: in flight = 2,000/s x 0.15 s = 300. If the fraud service slows to 2 s, the same traffic needs 4,000. Platform threads make that expensive; virtual threads make it cheap, which moves the question to what each of those requests is allowed to call.

sections.h: One virtual thread per request, and every limit written down
sections.html:
Lesson 2's pool runs the journal writes. Requests need threads too, and they spend almost all their time waiting: on the fraud service, on the limits service, on the ledger pool. The thread-per-request wall gave you the number: in flight = rate x time. At 2,000 requests a second and 150 ms each, 300 requests are in flight. When the fraud service slows to 2 s, 4,000 are. A platform thread per request would mean 4,000 OS threads, each with a 1 MB stack reserved, created at the worst possible moment.

Virtual threads make that number cheap. A request that waits on a socket, a latch or a semaphore unmounts from its carrier, and its stack waits on the heap, as How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations showed. So the server starts one new virtual thread per request, and never pools them:

Java
List<Reply> serveAll(List<Transfer> requests) throws Exception {
    try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        List<Future<Reply>> replies = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Transfer t : requests) replies.add(perRequest.submit(() -> handle(t)));   // 1. start every request
        List<Reply> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Future<Reply> f : replies) out.add(f.get());                             // 2. then wait, in order
        return out;
    }                                                                                  // 3. close() waits for all
}
Kotlin
fun serveAll(requests: List<Transfer>): List<Reply> =
    Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest ->
        val replies = requests.map { t -> perRequest.submit(Callable { handle(t) }) }   // 1. start every request
        replies.map { it.get() }                                                       // 2. then wait, in order
    }                                                                                   // 3. close() waits for all

In a real service the framework starts the threads: Quarkus with @RunOnVirtualThread, Spring Boot with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. What no framework does, as Moving a blocking service to virtual threads warned, is write your limits down. Unlimited threads mean unlimited calls to whatever sits behind them. So every scarce thing gets an explicit limit:

  • the fraud service: one shared Semaphore of 20 permits, held only around the fraud call;
  • the journal: lesson 2's bounded ledger- pool, 8 threads and 80 slots, which rejects with a 503 when it is full;
  • each request: one deadline of 300 ms for all of its screening.

The ledger pool stays a pool of platform threads on purpose. It isn't there to save thread creation. It is a limit with a queue and a rejection policy, around work you want bounded. Request threads wait for it with future.get(), and a parked virtual thread costs a little heap.

try.title: Do the arithmetic before the load test
steps: The fraud bulkhead has 20 permits, and a fraud call normally takes 20 ms. How many fraud checks a second can it pass? Is that enough for 400 requests a second? For 2,000?
During an outage each fraud call takes 2 s, but the request interrupts it at its 300 ms deadline. How many requests a second now get a permit at all, and what happens to the rest?
Open TransferServer.handle in the lab. Find the one wait that has no timeout and explain why it has none.
try.expect: Twenty permits at 20 ms pass at most 20 / 0.02 = 1,000 checks a second: plenty for 400, not enough for 2,000, so at 2,000 a second you'd need about 40 permits, if the fraud vendor allows that many. In the outage each permit is held for 300 ms, so only about 20 / 0.3 = 67 requests a second get one; the rest wait for a permit until their deadline and get the stand-in rule. The next section's demo shows exactly that. The wait without a timeout is ledger.submit(t).get(): once the ledger pool has accepted a transfer the money may move, and a timeout would end the wait but not the transfer.

sections.h: A bulkhead and a deadline for the slow fraud check
sections.html:
The fraud service is the slow, shared dependency. When it slows down, two things must not follow: every request waiting as long as it does, and every request piling onto it at once. A deadline stops the first, a bulkhead the second.

The bulkhead is the shared semaphore from Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores, with one change: the wait for a permit is bounded by the time the request has left.

Java
<T> T call(long waitNanos, Callable<T> block) throws Exception {
    if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS))   // 1. outside the try
        throw new TimeoutException("no permit in time");
    try {
        return block.call();                                      // 2. only the slow call holds it
    } finally {
        inFlight.release();                                       // 3. always given back
    }
}
Kotlin
fun <T> call(waitNanos: Long, block: () -> T): T {
    if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS))   // 1. outside the try
        throw TimeoutException("no permit in time")
    try {
        return block()                                            // 2. only the slow call holds it
    } finally {
        inFlight.release()                                        // 3. always given back
    }
}

The deadline is one number, computed once per request: System.nanoTime() + budget. Every wait inside the request uses what is left of it: the wait for a permit and the wait for the fraud answer. When it runs out, the request stops waiting and falls back. The fallback is a business rule, borrowed from card processing, called stand-in: small transfers (up to 50.00 here) go through without a fraud answer, larger ones get a fast "try again". The limit is a risk decision, not a technical one.

Stopping the wait is not enough. Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption made the point: a timeout on get ends your wait, not the task. A fraud call that runs on after its request has answered still holds a permit, and during an outage those orphans fill the bulkhead, so new requests can't get a permit even for a call that would succeed. So at the deadline the request interrupts the call. The interrupted call's finally gives the permit back, and the next request can use it. Give the fraud HTTP client its own timeout of the same length as well, so a call that ignores the interrupt still ends.

In this section's demo, an outage that makes every fraud call take 2 s still answers every request within about 320 ms, and the fraud service never sees more than 20 calls at once.

try.title: Take the fraud service down
steps: Run FraudOutageDemo (or FraudOutageDemoJava): 400 requests a second for 3 seconds, fraud calls take 20 ms. Predict the verdicts and the most fraud calls in flight.
Run it with -Pargs=outage, so every fraud call takes 2 s. Amounts are random up to 200.00 and the stand-in limit is 50.00. Predict the share of stand-ins and the slowest reply.
Delete the call.cancel(true) line and run the outage again. Predict first: what changes, and why?

code.title: FraudOutageDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l03.demo import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder private const val BUDGET_NANOS = 300_000_000L // every request answers within 300 ms private const val STAND_IN_CENTS = 5_000L // stand-in limit: up to 50.00 goes through unchecked private val permits = Semaphore(20) // the fraud bulkhead private val inFlight = AtomicInteger() private val mostInFlight = AtomicInteger() private val verdicts = ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder>() private val slowestMs = AtomicLong() // the fraud call, on its own virtual thread: a permit first, then the remote call private fun fraudCall(latencyMs: Long, deadline: Long): Boolean { if (!permits.tryAcquire(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) throw TimeoutException("no permit") try { mostInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) try { Thread.sleep(latencyMs) // the fraud service; an interrupt ends it early } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet() } return true } finally { permits.release() } } private fun screen(cents: Long, latencyMs: Long): String { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + BUDGET_NANOS Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perCall -> val call = perCall.submit(Callable { fraudCall(latencyMs, deadline) }) return try { if (call.get(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) "approved" else "declined" } catch (e: TimeoutException) { // our deadline passed first call.cancel(true) // interrupt the call: it holds a permit fallback(cents) } catch (e: ExecutionException) { // no permit before the deadline fallback(cents) } } } private fun fallback(cents: Long) = if (cents <= STAND_IN_CENTS) "stand-in" else "timed out" /** 400 requests a second for 3 seconds, each on its own virtual thread. Pass "outage" to slow the fraud service to 2 s. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val latencyMs = if (args.firstOrNull() == "outage") 2_000L else 20L Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> repeat(300) { // 300 rounds of 4 requests, 10 ms apart repeat(4) { val cents = 1 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(20_000) perRequest.execute { val t0 = System.nanoTime() verdicts.computeIfAbsent(screen(cents, latencyMs)) { LongAdder() }.increment() slowestMs.accumulateAndGet((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ::maxOf) } } Thread.sleep(10) } } println("fraud service takes $latencyMs ms: ${verdicts.toSortedMap()}") println("most fraud calls in flight: ${mostInFlight.get()}, slowest reply: ${slowestMs.get()} ms") }

Pass "outage" to slow the fraud service to 2 s. */ public class FraudOutageDemoJava { static final long BUDGET_NANOS = 300_000_000L; // every request answers within 300 ms static final long STAND_IN_CENTS = 5_000L; // stand-in limit: up to 50.00 goes through unchecked static final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20); // the fraud bulkhead static final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), mostInFlight = new AtomicInteger(); static final Map<String, LongAdder> verdicts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); static final AtomicLong slowestMs = new AtomicLong(); // the fraud call, on its own virtual thread: a permit first, then the remote call static boolean fraudCall(long latencyMs, long deadline) throws Exception { if (!permits.tryAcquire(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) throw new TimeoutException("no permit"); try { mostInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(latencyMs); // the fraud service; an interrupt ends it early } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet(); } return true; } finally { permits.release(); } } static String screen(long cents, long latencyMs) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + BUDGET_NANOS; try (ExecutorService perCall = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Boolean> call = perCall.submit(() -> fraudCall(latencyMs, deadline)); try { return call.get(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) ? "approved" : "declined"; } catch (TimeoutException e) { // our deadline passed first call.cancel(true); // interrupt the call: it holds a permit return fallback(cents); } catch (ExecutionException e) { // no permit before the deadline return fallback(cents); } } } static String fallback(long cents) { return cents <= STAND_IN_CENTS ? "stand-in" : "timed out"; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { long latencyMs = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("outage") ? 2_000 : 20; try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int round = 0; round < 300; round++) { // 300 rounds of 4 requests, 10 ms apart for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { long cents = 1 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(20_000); perRequest.execute(() -> { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { verdicts.computeIfAbsent(screen(cents, latencyMs), k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } slowestMs.accumulateAndGet((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, Math::max); }); } Thread.sleep(10); } } System.out.printf("fraud service takes %d ms: %s%n", latencyMs, new TreeMap<>(verdicts)); System.out.printf("most fraud calls in flight: %d, slowest reply: %d ms%n", mostInFlight.get(), slowestMs.get()); } }

try.expect: Normally all 1,200 are approved, with at most about 20 fraud calls in flight (Little's law says 400 x 0.02 = 8 on average; bursts go higher) and the slowest reply well under 100 ms. In the outage, about a quarter of the requests get the stand-in rule (290 of 1,200 in one run), the rest time out, the fraud service never sees more than 20 calls, and the slowest reply is about 320 ms. Without the cancel, the verdicts look the same, but the slowest reply is about 2,300 ms: each request's executor closes at the end of use, and close() waits for the fraud call nobody cancelled. With a shared executor instead, the replies would be on time and the orphaned calls would hold their permits for the full 2 s.

sections.h: Fail fast when one check says no
sections.html:
Screening calls two services: the fraud service, slow and behind the bulkhead, and the account limits service, which is fast. Run them at the same time and a request costs the slower of the two, not the sum. The trap is in how you collect the answers. Structured concurrency and scoped values showed it: call get() on the futures in the order you started them, and a fast "no" waits behind a slow "yes". In this section's demo the limits check says no at 10 ms, and the request still answers at about 600 ms.

Take the answers in the order they finish, and stop at the first no:

Java
Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException {
    long deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos();                // 1. one deadline for both checks
    ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    try {
        CompletionService<Boolean> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(perTask);
        done.submit(() -> fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime(), () -> fraud.passes(t)));   // 2. fork both
        done.submit(() -> limits.passes(t));
        for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
            Future<Boolean> next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS);
            if (next == null) return fallback(t);                        // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule
            try {
                if (!next.get()) return Verdict.DECLINED;                // 4. a check said no: fail fast
            } catch (ExecutionException e) {
                if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) return fallback(t);   // no fraud permit in time
                return Verdict.DECLINED;                                 // 4. a check failed: fail fast
            }
        }
        return Verdict.APPROVED;
    } finally {
        perTask.shutdownNow();                                           // 5. interrupt whatever still runs...
        perTask.close();                                                 //    ...and wait until those threads end
    }
}
Kotlin
fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict {
    val deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos()                 // 1. one deadline for both checks
    val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()
    try {
        val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask)
        done.submit { fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime()) { fraud.passes(t) } }   // 2. fork both
        done.submit { limits.passes(t) }
        repeat(2) {
            val next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
                ?: return fallback(t)                                    // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule
            val passed = try {
                next.get()
            } catch (e: ExecutionException) {
                if (e.cause is TimeoutException) return fallback(t)      //    no fraud permit in time
                return Verdict.DECLINED                                  // 4. a check failed: fail fast
            }
            if (!passed) return Verdict.DECLINED                         // 4. a check said no: fail fast
        }
        return Verdict.APPROVED
    } finally {
        perTask.shutdownNow()                                            // 5. interrupt whatever still runs...
        perTask.close()                                                  //    ...and wait until those threads end
    }
}

ExecutorCompletionService hands you each future as it completes, so the first no is seen at once, and so is the first exception. Either one declines the transfer. The finally is what makes it fail fast: shutdownNow() interrupts the check that is still running, and close() waits until its thread has really ended. That order matters, as the lab in that lesson showed: close() after shutdownNow() waits for threads, not for futures. So no check outlives its request, still holding a permit or writing a log line for a request that has already answered.

This is structured concurrency built by hand from an executor. JDK 25 has StructuredTaskScope for exactly this job, but it is a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27, so it stays out of the labs. The deeper note shows the same screening with it.

One rule binds every check: it has to stop when interrupted. sleep, locks, queues, latches and semaphores do. A check that computes in a loop and never looks at the interrupt flag keeps running, and close() waits for it, deadline or not.

try.title: Collect in order, then fail fast
steps: Run FailFastDemo. One transfer, two checks: fraud answers yes after 500 ms, limits answers no after 10 ms. Predict when each half prints its verdict.
In the fail-fast half, replace done.take() with the futures in submit order: keep the two futures that done.submit returns and call get() on them in that order. Run it again.

The limits check says no at 10 ms. When does the request get its answer? */ fun main() { println("in order: get() the fraud check, then the limits check") t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val fraud = perTask.submit(Callable { fraudCheck() }) val limits = perTask.submit(Callable { limitsCheck() }) val verdict = if (fraud.get() && limits.get()) "approved" else "declined" println(" %4d ms verdict: %s".format(ms(), verdict)) } println("fail fast: take results as they finish, stop the rest at the first no") t0 = System.nanoTime() val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() try { val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask) done.submit { fraudCheck() } done.submit { limitsCheck() } var verdict = "approved" for (i in 1..2) { if (!done.take().get()) { verdict = "declined"; break } // completion order, not submit order } println(" %4d ms verdict: %s".format(ms(), verdict)) } finally { perTask.shutdownNow() // interrupt the check nobody needs any more perTask.close() // and wait until its thread has ended } }

try.expect: Collected in order, the verdict comes after the fraud check answers, at about 500 to 600 ms, though the answer was known at 10 ms. Fail-fast prints declined at about 12 ms, and the fraud check reports interrupted 2 ms later, when shutdownNow() reaches it. After your change, the fail-fast half waits about 500 ms again: running checks in parallel only pays if you also collect them in completion order.

sections.h: Keep the carriers free: nothing slow under an account lock
sections.html:
Lesson 1 chose ReentrantLock for the accounts, and this is where that choice matters. A virtual thread is pinned when it blocks but can't leave its carrier, as Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps showed. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized, or waiting to enter a synchronized block another thread holds, pins. JDK 24 fixed both (JEP 491), and JDK 25 is the first LTS with the fix. These labs compile for JDK 21 and must run there too, so the ledger uses ReentrantLock, which has always let a waiting virtual thread unmount.

The lock type is the smaller half of the rule. The bigger half is that nothing slow happens while you hold an account lock. Here is what someone might write to make "journal and apply" one atomic step:

Java
synchronized (merchant) {          // or merchantLock.lock()
    journal.append(t);             // 20 ms of disk I/O while holding the lock
    merchant.credit(t.cents());
}
Kotlin
synchronized(merchant) {           // or merchantLock.withLock { }
    journal.append(t)              // 20 ms of disk I/O while holding the lock
    merchant.credit(t.cents)
}

The demo runs this with one carrier thread, 20 payments into one hot merchant account, and a ticker that wants to tick every 10 ms. With synchronized on JDK 21, the ticker missed 425 ms of ticks: the carrier was pinned the whole time, so nothing else ran. With ReentrantLock the ticker was fine, but the 20 payments still took 430 ms, one after another, because each held the lock for its whole disk write. That is Little's law again: a lock held for 20 ms lets through at most 50 payments a second. With the journal written first and the lock taken only for the credit, all 20 took 21 ms.

So the rule from synchronized and intrinsic locks holds in its strongest form. Inside an account lock, read and write the accounts, nothing else. The journal write, the fraud call and any logging that might block happen outside. That is why lesson 2's LedgerService writes the journal before apply takes a single lock.

To check a running service, keep JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event on; it records pins longer than 20 ms by default. The old -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads flag was removed in JDK 24.

code.title: LockScopeDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l03.demo import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.withLock private val merchantMonitor = Any() // a hot merchant account, guarded by a monitor... private val merchantLock = ReentrantLock() // ...or by a ReentrantLock private var merchantBalance = 0L private fun journalWrite() = Thread.sleep(20) // 20 ms of blocking I/O /** * One carrier thread. 20 virtual threads pay a hot merchant account while a ticker tries to tick * every 10 ms. Where the journal write sits decides whether the carrier stays free. */ fun main() { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", "1") // before the first virtual thread println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, 1 carrier thread") runVariant("journal inside synchronized ") { synchronized(merchantMonitor) { journalWrite(); merchantBalance += 100 } } runVariant("journal inside ReentrantLock ") { merchantLock.withLock { journalWrite(); merchantBalance += 100 } } runVariant("journal first, then the lock ") { journalWrite(); merchantLock.withLock { merchantBalance += 100 } } } private fun runVariant(label: String, transfer: () -> Unit) { var longestGap = 0L val ticker = Thread.ofVirtual().start { var last = System.nanoTime() repeat(40) { Thread.sleep(10) val now = System.nanoTime() longestGap = maxOf(longestGap, (now - last) / 1_000_000) last = now } } Thread.sleep(5) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val payers = List(20) { Thread.ofVirtual().start(transfer) } payers.forEach { it.join() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 ticker.join() println("$label 20 transfers in %4d ms, longest gap between ticks: %3d ms".format(ms, longestGap)) }

alt.title: LockScopeDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * One carrier thread. 20 virtual threads pay a hot merchant account while a ticker tries to tick * every 10 ms. Where the journal write sits decides whether the carrier stays free. */ public class LockScopeDemoJava { static final Object merchantMonitor = new Object(); // a hot merchant account, guarded by a monitor... static final ReentrantLock merchantLock = new ReentrantLock(); // ...or by a ReentrantLock static long merchantBalance = 0; static volatile long longestGap; static void journalWrite() { // 20 ms of blocking I/O try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.setProperty("jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism", "1"); // before the first virtual thread System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version() + ", 1 carrier thread"); runVariant("journal inside synchronized ", () -> { synchronized (merchantMonitor) { journalWrite(); merchantBalance += 100; } }); runVariant("journal inside ReentrantLock ", () -> { merchantLock.lock(); try { journalWrite(); merchantBalance += 100; } finally { merchantLock.unlock(); } }); runVariant("journal first, then the lock ", () -> { journalWrite(); merchantLock.lock(); try { merchantBalance += 100; } finally { merchantLock.unlock(); } }); } static void runVariant(String label, Runnable transfer) throws InterruptedException { longestGap = 0; Thread ticker = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { long last = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long now = System.nanoTime(); longestGap = Math.max(longestGap, (now - last) / 1_000_000); last = now; } }); Thread.sleep(5); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<Thread> payers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) payers.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(transfer)); for (Thread p : payers) p.join(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; ticker.join(); System.out.printf("%s 20 transfers in %4d ms, longest gap between ticks: %3d ms%n", label, ms, longestGap); } }

try.expect: On JDK 21 (the run here): synchronized took 426 ms with a 425 ms gap in the ticks, because the pinned carrier couldn't run the ticker. ReentrantLock took 433 ms with a 19 ms gap: the carrier was free, but the payments queued behind a lock held across I/O. Journal first took 21 ms with a 16 ms gap. On JDK 24 and later, JEP 491 lets a virtual thread that holds a monitor unmount, so the first row's gap should drop to the second row's, while its time stays near 430 ms: the fix removes the pinning, not the queue behind the lock.

refs.title: JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning

sections.h: Read 10,000 virtual threads in a JSON dump
sections.html:
Lesson 2 found a hung pool with jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Run that on the server during a fraud outage and the request threads are not there. On JDK 21, Thread.print lists platform threads only. JDK 24 added the virtual threads that are mounted at that moment, which during an outage is almost none. A parked virtual thread is a stack on the heap, not an OS thread, so the classic dump never sees it.

The dump for virtual threads is Thread.dump_to_file:

jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/requests.json

Here is the demo's dump of 10,000 parked requests on JDK 21, cut down to its shape:

{"threadDump": {
  "processId": "29205",
  "runtimeVersion": "21.0.12.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu",
  "threadContainers": [
    {"container": "<root>", "parent": null, "owner": null, "threadCount": "7",
     "threads": [{"tid": "1", "name": "main",
                  "stack": ["java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep0(Native Method)", "..."]}, "..."]},
    {"container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@7cded998", "parent": "<root>",
     "owner": null, "threadCount": "10000",
     "threads": [
       {"tid": "19", "name": "request-0", "stack": [
         "java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:596)",
         "...",
         "java.base/java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch.await(CountDownLatch.java:230)",
         "workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:14)",
         "..."]},
       "...",
       {"tid": "10025", "name": "request-9999", "stack": [
         "java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:596)",
         "...",
         "java.base/java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.acquire(Semaphore.java:318)",
         "workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:12)",
         "..."]}]},
    {"container": "ForkJoinPool-1/jdk.internal.vm.SharedThreadContainer@3ee32429",
     "parent": "<root>", "owner": null, "threadCount": "4",
     "threads": [{"tid": "20", "name": "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1", "stack": ["..."]}, "..."]},
    "... three empty containers ..."
  ]}}

Threads sit in thread containers. A container is whatever started them: your executor, with its own entry and thread list, or <root> for ordinary platform threads such as main. The 10,000 requests are one container, the carriers another (ForkJoinPool-1, one worker per core). On JDK 21 each thread entry has only tid, name and stack. JDK 25 adds state, virtual, parkBlocker and carrier. The named factory, Thread.ofVirtual().name("request-", 0), is what gives you request-9999 instead of an empty name.

Ten thousand stacks can't be read one at a time, so group them. Count threads per container, then count stacks by the frame where your code starts and the JDK frame just above it:

jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threads | length)\t\(.container)"' /tmp/requests.json

jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[].stack
       | (map(startswith("workbench.")) | index(true)) as $i
       | select($i != null and $i > 0)
       | "\(.[$i-1]) <- \(.[$i])"' /tmp/requests.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

   9980 java.base/java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.acquire(Semaphore.java:318) <- workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:12)
     20 java.base/java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch.await(CountDownLatch.java:230) <- workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:14)
      1 java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509) <- workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.main(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:34)

That is the outage in three lines: 20 requests are inside the fraud call, 9,980 wait for a fraud permit, and main sleeps. The bulkhead held, and the fraud service is the problem. A dump of 10,000 threads is about 12 MB, so write it to a file and read it with tools, never in a terminal.

try.title: Dump 10,000 parked requests
steps: Run ParkedRequestsDemo (or ParkedRequestsDemoJava) with -Pargs=60. It starts 10,000 requests on named virtual threads that all wait for a fraud service that hangs, and prints its PID.
In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print and look for request- threads.
Run jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/requests.json, then the two jq commands from this section. To take a second dump, delete the file first or add -overwrite.
Before you read the counts, predict them: how many requests are inside the fraud call, and how many wait for a permit?

code.title: ParkedRequestsDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ledger.l03.demo import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore private val fraudPermits = Semaphore(20) // the fraud bulkhead: 20 calls at once private val fraudDown = CountDownLatch(1) // the fraud service hangs until this opens private fun handle(id: Int): String { fraudPermits.acquire() // 9,980 requests park here... try { fraudDown.await() // ...and 20 park here, inside the "fraud call" return "request $id: ok" } finally { fraudPermits.release() } } /** * 10,000 requests, one named virtual thread each, all stuck behind a fraud service that hangs. * Take a JSON thread dump while they are parked. Arg: seconds to stay parked (default 3). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val seconds = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 3 val named = Thread.ofVirtual().name("request-", 0).factory() // request-0, request-1, ... in the dump val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(named).use { perRequest -> val replies = List(10_000) { id -> perRequest.submit(Callable { handle(id) }) } val pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid() println("pid $pid: 10,000 requests parked for $seconds s. In another terminal:") println(" jcmd $pid Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/requests.json") Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L) fraudDown.countDown() // the fraud service comes back replies.forEach { it.get() } } println("all 10,000 answered after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") }

alt.title: ParkedRequestsDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.ledger.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** * 10,000 requests, one named virtual thread each, all stuck behind a fraud service that hangs. * Take a JSON thread dump while they are parked. Arg: seconds to stay parked (default 3). */ public class ParkedRequestsDemoJava { static final Semaphore fraudPermits = new Semaphore(20); // the fraud bulkhead: 20 calls at once static final CountDownLatch fraudDown = new CountDownLatch(1); // the fraud service hangs until this opens static String handle(int id) throws InterruptedException { fraudPermits.acquire(); // 9,980 requests park here... try { fraudDown.await(); // ...and 20 park here, inside the "fraud call" return "request " + id + ": ok"; } finally { fraudPermits.release(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int seconds = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 3; ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofVirtual().name("request-", 0).factory(); // request-0, request-1, ... long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(named)) { List<Future<String>> replies = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) { int id = i; replies.add(perRequest.submit(() -> handle(id))); } long pid = ProcessHandle.current().pid(); System.out.printf("pid %d: 10,000 requests parked for %d s. In another terminal:%n", pid, seconds); System.out.printf(" jcmd %d Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/requests.json%n", pid); Thread.sleep(seconds * 1_000L); fraudDown.countDown(); // the fraud service comes back for (Future<String> f : replies) f.get(); } System.out.printf("all 10,000 answered after %d ms%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } }

try.expect: Thread.print shows no request- thread at all on JDK 21: only main, the four ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N carriers and JVM threads. The JSON file is about 12 MB with six containers: 10,000 threads under the ThreadPerTaskExecutor, four carriers under ForkJoinPool-1, main and a few JVM threads under <root>, and three empty ones. Grouped by stack: 9,980 in Semaphore.acquire at line 12, 20 in CountDownLatch.await at line 14, and main in Thread.sleep. The Java twin shows the same counts with ParkedRequestsDemoJava.handle. On JDK 25 every entry also carries its state and "virtual": true.

analogy: The server is a restaurant that seats every guest the moment they walk in, because chairs (virtual threads) cost almost nothing. What it rations is what sits behind the chairs. The sommelier (the fraud service) takes 20 guests at a time. The kitchen (the ledger pool) has 8 cooks and 80 order slips, and when the slips run out the door says "kitchen full, try again in a minute". Every guest is promised an answer within five minutes. A guest who has waited that long for the sommelier gets the house wine if the order is small and is asked to come back if it is large, and the sommelier is told to stop decanting for him. The analogy breaks at the chairs: a seated guest still takes floor space and a waiter's attention. A parked virtual thread takes a couple of kilobytes of heap and no thread at all until something wakes it.
world: This is the shape of a Quarkus payment endpoint with @RunOnVirtualThread: the request runs on a virtual thread and calls a fraud REST client, a limits client and the database. Quarkus adds neither the bulkhead nor the deadline. SmallRye Fault Tolerance's @Bulkhead and @Timeout are one way to declare them, and a shared Semaphore plus one deadline per request is another. Either way, size the bulkhead from the fraud vendor's concurrency limit and Little's law, and set the REST client's read timeout to the same budget. The stand-in limit is a risk decision: agree the amount with the risk team, and log every stand-in with its transfer id so it can be reviewed. During an incident, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json inside the pod tells you in a minute whether requests are stuck on your bulkhead or on something else.
mistake: The most common mistake is a timeout that ends the wait but not the work: future.get(300, MILLISECONDS) in a try, a fallback in the catch, and nothing that stops the call. Every request answers on time, so the dashboards look fine. Meanwhile each abandoned call keeps its bulkhead permit, its connection and its socket until the slow service answers, and during an outage those orphans fill the bulkhead, so even calls that would succeed can't get a permit. People make it because get with a timeout reads like a deadline. Cancel what you stopped waiting for (cancel(true), or shutdownNow() on the request's executor), release the permit in the call's own finally, and give the client library a timeout of the same length as a backstop.

compare.title: The request handler and the fan-in, in both languages

java.title: TransferServer.java
java.html: Reply handle(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException { Verdict verdict = screening.screen(t); if (verdict == Verdict.DECLINED) return new Reply(t.id(), Status.DECLINED, false); if (verdict == Verdict.TIMED_OUT) return new Reply(t.id(), Status.TIMED_OUT, false); Outcome outcome; try { outcome = ledger.submit(t).get(); // no timeout: the money may already be moving } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { return new Reply(t.id(), Status.BUSY, false); } Status status = outcome == Outcome.APPLIED ? Status.APPLIED : Status.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; return new Reply(t.id(), status, verdict == Verdict.STAND_IN); } List<Reply> serveAll(List<Transfer> requests) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Reply>> replies = new ArrayList<>(); for (Transfer t : requests) replies.add(perRequest.submit(() -> handle(t))); List<Reply> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Reply> f : replies) out.add(f.get()); return out; } }

kotlin.title: TransferServer.kt
kotlin.html: fun handle(t: Transfer): Reply { val verdict = screening.screen(t) if (verdict == Verdict.DECLINED) return Reply(t.id(), Status.DECLINED) if (verdict == Verdict.TIMED_OUT) return Reply(t.id(), Status.TIMED_OUT) val outcome = try { ledger.submit(t).get() // no timeout: the money may already be moving } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { return Reply(t.id(), Status.BUSY) } val status = if (outcome == Outcome.APPLIED) Status.APPLIED else Status.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS return Reply(t.id(), status, standIn = verdict == Verdict.STAND_IN) } fun serveAll(requests: List<Transfer>): List<Reply> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> val replies = requests.map { t -> perRequest.submit(Callable { handle(t) }) } replies.map { it.get() } }

compare.note: The threads, executors and futures are the same JDK classes on both sides; what differs is how each language spells the edges. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so get()'s InterruptedException and ExecutionException need no throws clause; an interrupted request thread still throws out of handle. A try is an expression in Kotlin, which lets val outcome = try { ... } replace Java's assign-in-try. use on an ExecutorService is Kotlin's try-with-resources, and both call close(), which waits for every request. Kotlin's default argument (standIn = false) saves the third constructor argument that the Java record needs every time. In the lab, the Kotlin server calls the Java ledger from lesson 2 directly: same package, same module, and records' accessors such as t.id() work as ordinary methods.

worked.title: Review a screening that passes the happy-path test

steps.say: A teammate's first version of screening. It passes the test where both checks answer in 20 ms. Before reading on, find what goes wrong when the fraud service takes 2 s and when the limits check says no.
steps.code: private val checkPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20) // "the bulkhead" fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict { val fraud = checkPool.submit(Callable { fraudClient.passes(t) }) val limits = checkPool.submit(Callable { limitsClient.passes(t) }) return try { if (fraud.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) && limits.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) Verdict.APPROVED else Verdict.DECLINED } catch (e: TimeoutException) { Verdict.STAND_IN } }

alt.html: private final ExecutorService checkPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20); // "the bulkhead" Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws Exception { Future<Boolean> fraud = checkPool.submit(() -> fraudClient.passes(t)); Future<Boolean> limits = checkPool.submit(() -> limitsClient.passes(t)); try { return fraud.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) && limits.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) ? Verdict.APPROVED : Verdict.DECLINED; } catch (TimeoutException e) { return Verdict.STAND_IN; } }

steps.say: Five problems, each from an earlier lesson. The pool caps the whole task, so in a fraud outage the limits checks queue behind stuck fraud calls: put the limit on the resource, not on a pool. Two timeouts of 300 ms in a row allow 600 ms: there is no single deadline. A fast no from limits waits behind the fraud answer: no fail-fast. On timeout nothing is cancelled, so the orphaned calls keep all 20 pool threads busy and the next requests time out before they even start. And every timeout becomes a stand-in, whatever the amount.

The fix is the lab's screen. Each numbered comment answers one problem: a deadline computed once (1), the fraud call alone behind a shared semaphore whose wait uses the time left (2), the stand-in rule only for small amounts (3), completion order and an early return for fail-fast (4), and shutdownNow() plus close() so nothing outlives the request (5).
steps.code: fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos() // 1. one deadline for both checks val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() try { val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask) done.submit { fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime()) { fraud.passes(t) } } // 2. fork both done.submit { limits.passes(t) } repeat(2) { val next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) ?: return fallback(t) // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule val passed = try { next.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { if (e.cause is TimeoutException) return fallback(t) // no fraud permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check failed: fail fast } if (!passed) return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check said no: fail fast } return Verdict.APPROVED } finally { perTask.shutdownNow() // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close() // ...and wait until those threads end } }

alt.html: Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos(); // 1. one deadline for both checks ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); try { CompletionService<Boolean> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(perTask); done.submit(() -> fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime(), () -> fraud.passes(t))); // 2. fork both done.submit(() -> limits.passes(t)); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { Future<Boolean> next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); if (next == null) return fallback(t); // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule try { if (!next.get()) return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check said no: fail fast } catch (ExecutionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) return fallback(t); // no fraud permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check failed: fail fast } } return Verdict.APPROVED; } finally { perTask.shutdownNow(); // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close(); // ...and wait until those threads end } }

steps.say: Check it against the lab's tests, which are the production behaviours you care about. A stuck fraud call ends at the deadline, is interrupted, and gives its permit back. A no from either check declines at once and interrupts the other. A full bulkhead means the fallback without calling the fraud service at all. And 10,000 concurrent requests never put more than 50 calls into the fraud service, while every APPLIED reply, replayed on the opening balances, gives exactly the ledger's final snapshot.

lab.title: Serve the ledger: a virtual thread per request, a bulkhead, a deadline, fail-fast
steps: Run the tests once. All ten fail. This lab is in Kotlin. The ledger underneath is lesson 2's Java solution, unchanged, in the same package. Read TransferServer.handle: it is written for you, and its one wait without a timeout is deliberate.
Write Bulkhead.call: tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) before the try, throw TimeoutException if it returns false, run block() inside the try, and release() in finally.

Write Screening.screen in the four steps of its KDoc: one deadline, an ExecutorCompletionService over a fresh virtual-thread executor, two polls with the time left, and shutdownNow() then close() in a finally.
Write TransferServer.serveAll: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { }, every request submitted before the first get().
Run the tests until all ten pass, then twice more. The slowest one sends 10,000 requests through the whole stack and replays every APPLIED reply against the final balances.
hints: return inside repeat { } or inside a try expression returns from screen itself, because repeat is inline. ?: return fallback(t) after poll handles the deadline in one line.
If the fail-fast tests time out, you are waiting for both checks. Take the futures from poll on the completion service, not the ones submit returned, in order.
If a test says a permit didn't come back, check that release() is in a finally and that tryAcquire is outside the try.
If the virtual-thread test reports hundreds of new platform threads, you used a pool. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts one new virtual thread per task.
lab.done: All ten tests in TransferServerTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the fail-fast fan-out with a deadline from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write fun firstNoWins(checks: List<() -> Boolean>, budget: Duration): Boolean?. It runs every check on its own virtual thread and returns false at the first false or exception, true if all pass, and null if the budget runs out first. No check may still be running when it returns.

answer.html: fun firstNoWins(checks: List<() -> Boolean>, budget: Duration): Boolean? { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos() // 1. one deadline val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() try { val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask) checks.forEach { check -> done.submit { check() } } // 2. fork them all repeat(checks.size) { val next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) ?: return null // 3. out of time val ok = try { next.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { false } if (!ok) return false // 4. the first no wins } return true } finally { perTask.shutdownNow() // 5. stop the rest... perTask.close() // ...and wait until they have ended } }

alt.html: Boolean firstNoWins(List<Callable<Boolean>> checks, Duration budget) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos(); // 1. one deadline ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); try { CompletionService<Boolean> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(perTask); for (Callable<Boolean> check : checks) done.submit(check); // 2. fork them all for (int i = 0; i < checks.size(); i++) { Future<Boolean> next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); if (next == null) return null; // 3. out of time boolean ok; try { ok = next.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ok = false; } if (!ok) return false; // 4. the first no wins } return true; } finally { perTask.shutdownNow(); // 5. stop the rest... perTask.close(); // ...and wait until they have ended } }

recap: One new virtual thread per request, never pooled. Write every limit down instead: a shared semaphore per slow dependency, a bounded pool for the journal, one deadline per request.
The bulkhead's permit wait and the call itself both use the time the request has left. At the deadline, interrupt the call, so its finally gives the permit back.
Fail fast: take results in completion order, decline at the first no or failure, then shutdownNow() and close() so no check outlives its request.
A fallback is a business rule: stand-in for small amounts, a fast "try again" for the rest. Never time out the wait for the ledger, because the money may already be moving.
Nothing slow inside an account lock. On JDK 21, blocking under synchronized pins the carrier; ReentrantLock doesn't pin, but a lock held across I/O still queues everyone behind it.
Thread.print doesn't show parked virtual threads. Thread.dump_to_file -format=json groups them by container; count them by stack with jq.

explain.prompt: Design review. A sceptical principal engineer has read the whole ledger, all three lessons of it, and asks: "Why virtual threads and a thread pool in the same service? Why 20 fraud permits and not 200? What happens to the money when the fraud service is down, when the pod is killed, and when two pods run this code?" Defend your design, and say plainly what it does not handle.
explain.answer:
Requests mostly wait, on the fraud service, the limits service and the ledger, so each one gets its own virtual thread: Little's law says about 300 are in flight normally and thousands in an outage, and a parked virtual thread costs a little heap. The ledger pool is not there to save threads. It is the write path's limit: 8 platform threads because 1,600 transfers a second at 5 ms of journal write is 8 in flight, 80 queue slots because that is 50 ms of waiting, and a counted rejection that turns overload into a 503 the client retries with the same transfer id.

The 20 permits come from the fraud vendor's concurrency limit and Little's law: at 20 ms a call they pass about 1,000 checks a second, above our peak. If the vendor allows more, the number goes up; it belongs to the downstream, not to us. When the fraud service is down, every request still answers within its 300 ms deadline: the bulkhead caps what the vendor sees, the deadline interrupts calls so their permits come back, and the stand-in rule approves small amounts and refuses the rest. Money only moves through apply, which keeps the three invariants under per-account locks taken in id order, so a stand-in can't break the books; it only takes a fraud risk we chose on purpose.

When the pod is killed, lesson 2's shutdown drains the pool or hands back the transfers that never started, so nothing accepted vanishes, as long as the journal is durable. What this design doesn't handle is everything that needs shared state. Two pods each have their own in-memory ledger, and their locks protect nothing across pods. A retry after a crash needs the journal replayed and an idempotency check on the transfer id. A production version keeps balances in the database, with row locks in id order or one owner per account, and keeps the rest of this design as it is.

deeper.html:
What a production version of this ledger adds, roughly in the order I'd build it:

  • Durable state: balances and the journal in a database, row locks taken in account id order or one owner per account, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint, and a unique key on the transfer id.
  • Idempotent replies: store each transfer's outcome by id, so a retry after a 503 or a client timeout gets the original answer instead of a second transfer.
  • Metrics on every limit: bulkhead permits in use and the wait for them, stand-ins, the ledger queue's size and rejections, time in queue, journal write latency, and JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events.
  • A circuit breaker in front of the fraud service, so that during an outage requests go to the stand-in rule at once instead of each one waiting out its deadline.
  • Request context, such as the request id, in a scoped value (final in JDK 25) or passed as a parameter, so it reaches every log line on every virtual thread.
  • Load tests with real latency distributions, and a fault-injection run where the fraud service hangs, checked against the same invariants as the lab's tests.

Structured concurrency is the JDK's own version of screen. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505) and still preview in JDK 26 and 27; JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28 with the JDK 27 API. Here is the screening in the JDK 25 shape. It needs --enable-preview, which is why it isn't in the labs:

Java
// JDK 25, preview: javac --release 25 --enable-preview ... and java --enable-preview ...
Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Boolean>awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(),
            cf -> cf.withTimeout(budget))) {
        scope.fork(() -> { if (!fraudBulkhead.call(budget.toNanos(), () -> fraud.passes(t))) throw new Declined(); return true; });
        scope.fork(() -> { if (!limits.passes(t)) throw new Declined(); return true; });
        scope.join();                                  // the first failure cancels the other subtask
        return Verdict.APPROVED;
    } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) {
        return fallback(t);                            // the scope has cancelled both subtasks
    } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) {
        return e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException ? fallback(t) : Verdict.DECLINED;
    }
}
Kotlin
// JDK 25, preview: compile and run with --enable-preview
fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict = try {
    StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow<Boolean>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(budget) }.use { scope ->
        scope.fork(Callable { if (!fraudBulkhead.call(budget.toNanos()) { fraud.passes(t) }) throw Declined(); true })
        scope.fork(Callable { if (!limits.passes(t)) throw Declined(); true })
        scope.join()                                   // the first failure cancels the other subtask
        Verdict.APPROVED
    }
} catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException) {
    fallback(t)                                        // the scope has cancelled both subtasks
} catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) {
    if (e.cause is TimeoutException) fallback(t) else Verdict.DECLINED
}

A "no" becomes an exception (Declined, your own small exception class), because the default joiner fails fast on exceptions, not on values. The scope's close() cancels and waits for every subtask, which is what your finally did by hand, and the JSON thread dump shows each scope as its own container under the request that opened it. In JDK 27 the built-in joiners throw ExecutionException instead of FailedException, so that catch changes when you move.
